The locomotive was driven into the shed after the day's final run.
i verksted eller remise for reparasjon
in a workshop or locomotive shed for repairs

1000994.etyen:
Borrowed from French remise (“putting back; storage, shed”), a substantivization of the feminine singular past participle of remettre (“to put back, put away”). Remettre is inherited through Old French remetre (“to put back, replace”) from Latin remittō (“send back; let go; remit”), from re- (“back, again”) + mittō (“send, let go”). Mittō is probably from Proto-Italic *meitō (“send, put forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“change, exchange; remove, send”).
The French noun originally denotes something “put back” or “put away”, hence a place where vehicles are put away when not in use.

1004578.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse -ði (“weak-verb simple-past ending”), containing the inherited Germanic dental preterite marker. In Bokmål, it appears as -dde after certain verb stems, commonly with shortening of a preceding long vowel.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -dde and Swedish -dde (“weak-verb simple-past ending”).

of those [i.e. the convicts under Louis XIV] who worked at the dockyard, some worked in the sail loft, others in the ropewalk, but most spun, wove and sewed clothing for the navy

1004834.etyen:
From seil (“sail”) + -makeri (“activity- or workshop-forming suffix”), literally “sail-making activity or workshop”; compare seilmaker (“sailmaker”).
The suffix -makeri (“activity- or workshop-forming suffix”) is from Middle Low German -makerie, from maken (“to make, do”); compare -eri (“activity-, process-, or place-forming suffix”).
Compare Danish sejlmageri and Swedish segelmakeri (“sailmaking; sail loft”).
